prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: optical lattice clocks, credited to Katori and Ye, as the only prize part. After reading the full first-round exchange, the case still rests on three points. First, the invention is specific and separable: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping thousands of atoms, and Ye's strontium systems, comparisons and many-body clock work took the uncertainty to the 10^-18 level. Second, the result is mature and independently confirmed at JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB and SYRTE and in more than one species, so it does not depend on a single group's claim. Third, it has already produced measurements, namely tests of relativity and of the constancy of constants, relativistic geodesy and dark-matter searches, so the prize can be justified on demonstrated capability and does not need the redefinition of the second to have happened. Six of eight members place it first with the same two names, which I treat as a sign that the scientific objections have been tested and have not found a flaw, not as a reason in itself. I would write the citation around the lattice clock and magic-wavelength trapping, so that it is plainly distinct from the frequency-comb prize of 2005.
statement.case_against: The reservations I take seriously are unchanged. Precision spectroscopy has had prizes in 1989, 2005 and 2012, and a committee can reasonably ask whether a fourth in the neighbourhood is a rotation too few. I judge that a presentational point, because the lattice clock answers a different problem from the comb (interrogating many neutral atoms without motional shifts, not counting optical cycles), but I cannot show that it is not a matter of taste. Two names also leave out Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups at NIST and PTB, and the citation can only acknowledge this, not fix it. Third, the case is partly about a measurement capability and not a new phenomenon, which Eriksson argues is a lesser kind of discovery; I think the criterion covers inventions of this type, but a committee that reads it more narrowly would be entitled to prefer B017.

responses.point: Eriksson asks whether my ranking of B017 behind B001 is a scientific objection or only about maturity, and argues that twisted bilayer graphene opened a new class of correlated matter while the clocks refine a capability whose basis is already recognised.
responses.response: It is mainly maturity and attribution, not doubt about the physics. I accept that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the 2018 experiments are a clean theory-to-experiment case and that the pairing mechanism being unsettled does not by itself bear on the merit of the discovery, as he and Danielsson argue. Where I still differ is that the correlated-insulator and superconducting states have been studied for about eight years, the first author Cao and several groups are outside the credited names, and the group-leader convention has to carry real weight. On his point that the clocks only refine recognised physics, I disagree: laser cooling, trapping and the comb are tools, but magic-wavelength trapping is a new idea that made a new type of clock possible, and the factor of roughly 100 over the caesium standard is a change of regime in measurement, not an incremental refinement. I would not call B017 wrong and I keep it as a later-year candidate and as an alternative.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether I regard the relative weight of Katori and Ye as an obstacle to a two-name citation, and wants a frank discussion of the credit gap.
responses.response: I do not see the relative weight as an obstacle. Katori's contribution is the concept and its first demonstrations, and Ye's is the record-accuracy strontium systems and the clock-comparison and many-body work; these are different contributions of comparable decisiveness, and the citation can name both by wording it as invention and development. The credit gap is real, because Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley made essential steps, but the three-person limit applies to every shortlisted part, and a two-name part is the smaller exposure on the table. I also agree with her that the overlap with Hall's 2005 prize deserves frank discussion, and I would settle it in the citation by naming magic-wavelength trapping explicitly.

responses.point: Pearce keeps IceCube (Halzen alone) as a second part but says a clocks-only prize is cleaner and that he would drop B027 if colleagues find the single-name credit unconvincing; he also says the redefinition of the second should not be needed to justify the prize.
responses.response: I agree with him on timing: the case rests on the instrument and what it has already measured. On the second part I remain unconvinced, and I think this is the right moment to say so plainly. A one-name credit for a collaboration-scale project leaves out early proposers, detector builders and analysts, and the source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are less secure than the diffuse flux. He concedes both points himself, and I think adding a weakly supported part would dilute the clocks, not strengthen them. I recognise neutrino astronomy as a genuine new observational window and would be glad to see it again once the credit can be spread over more names or the source evidence is firmer.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B017 first, says the committee could state openly that experimental credit goes to the group through its leader, and says he cannot judge the clock case from outside the field.
responses.response: I take his invitation to say what would move me: independent reproduction of the correlated and superconducting phases across several groups is already largely there, so what would move me is a settled view of the superconducting mechanism, or at least a clearer account of which experiments identify the credit among Jarillo-Herrero, Cao and the other groups. Since he says he cannot assess the clocks from outside, I can supply the relevant check from inside: the 10^-18 figure is not one group's estimate but comes from clock comparisons between independent laboratories, and that is the strongest evidence of maturity that any shortlisted part has. I would not object if the committee chose B017 first, but I think it is less secure this year than B001.

responses.point: Olsson also ranks the clocks first and treats the 1989, 2005 and 2012 precedents as the main reservation, together with the narrower two-person credit.
responses.response: I agree that the precedents are the strongest counter-argument and I do not regard them as a bar. The 2012 prize recognised the control of single trapped quantum systems and the 2005 prize the comb and coherent spectroscopy; neither addresses neutral atoms in a magic lattice. I would add that the chair's question about whether any member treats the precedents as a bar has so far drawn no such answer in the exchange, and I do not either, but I would accept that a committee could weigh them differently.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards a fourth prize in precision spectroscopy and atomic clocks as a rotation too few, in which case B042 or B017 would be the natural alternative.
Whether two names are enough credit given the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups, and how much the citation can acknowledge them.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be treated as a condition for timing; I think not, but I cannot rule out that others reasonably will.
Whether the case for B017 will be materially stronger in a year or two, once the pairing mechanism and the experimental credit are better settled.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I record again that my doctoral period included a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and that Jun Ye's work grows out of the JILA comb and laser-stabilisation tradition associated with Hall. I also work in laser stabilisation and precision optical spectroscopy, and I have Lund colleagues and European quantum-memory collaborations that do not include any credited name. The profile documents no collaboration, supervision or institutional tie with Katori or Ye, so I do not consider the link a ground for recusal, but in answer to the chair's question I leave the judgement to the committee and will accept discounting of my B001 position if it decides that is appropriate. I note that B001 does not depend on my position, since five other members prefer it independently.
